title: Dense prediction: segmentation
text:
Dense prediction: segmentation
Goal
• Input: image (H × W × 3) (or feature map in the network).
• Output: a class label per pixel (or per location): mask of size
H′ × W ′ × C (often H′ =H, W ′ =W ).
Encoder–decoder idea
• Encoder: stack of Conv2d (+ pooling / stride) ⇒smaller spatial maps,
larger receptive field, semantic features.
• Decoder: need to go back to full resolution (or to resolution aligned
with the image) to assign a label to each pixel.
• Upsampling of feature maps is therefore central.

title: Common decoder ingredients
text:
Common decoder ingredients
Ways to increase spatial size
• Fixed interpolation: e.g. nearest / bilinear upsample, then Conv2d to
mix channels.
• Transposed convolution: a conv-like layer that increases spatial size
(“inverse stride” in a precise sense) with learned filters.
• Combinations: in many net designs, several transposed (or strided)
blocks in sequence, often with skip connections (e.g. U-Net).
Vocabulary
Names you may see: ConvTranspose2d, deconv (colloquial), fractionally
strided convolution, upconv, upconvolution. “Deconvolution” in math ̸=
this; avoid confusion in papers.

What transposed Conv2d does (intuition)

title: Intuition: reverse the forward of a strided Conv2d
text:
Intuition: reverse the forward of a strided Conv2d
Standard Conv2d with s > 1
• Forward: from an input X, produces an output with smaller
Hout × Wout (when s > 1), in one layer.
• The associated adjoint / VJP pattern for backprop (how gradients
spread from Y to X) has a “scatter-add” + conv structure: it is
formally what transposed conv implements when configured correctly.
Transposed conv in practice (decoder block)
• Think of a layer that maps
Z ∈RB×Cin×Hin×Win ⇒Y ∈RB×Cout×Hout×Wout with Hout ≥Hin when
s > 1 (and padding / output padding as chosen).
• Learned kernel parameters (unlike fixed bilinear).
Takeaway

title: Relation to Conv2d (one sentence)
text:
Relation to Conv2d (one sentence)
Duality
The operator implemented by ConvTranspose2d in PyTorch (with a given
k, s, p, . . . ) is the transposed of a Conv2d (with a related shape
configuration) w.r.t. the Frobenius inner product on the flattened feature
maps. That is why the tensor shape “runs backward” in the H, W story
compared to a standard strided conv.
Consequence for implementation
If you have an encoder block that strided a map by factor f with a Conv2d
design, a decoder that “unstrides“ by a matching factor is often set up with
ConvTranspose2d of compatible hyperparameters, sometimes paired with
skip fusion (U-Net) when channels/spatial resolution must be aligned.

title: Output height and width: PyTorch (dilation = 1)
text:
Output height and width: PyTorch (dilation = 1)
torch.nn.ConvTranspose2d
For each spatial axis (same for H and W ) with dilation=1:
Hout = (Hin−1)·stride−2·padding+kernel size - 1+output padding+1.
(Equivalent formula in PyTorch documentation; check version when in doubt.)
“Fractionally strided” picture
stride > 1 ⇒Hout > Hin in typical default settings,
so feature maps are enlarged in the forward pass of this layer.

title: Roles of the main parameters
text:
Roles of the main parameters
kernel size (k)
• As in Conv2d, defines a local k × k (per-channel structure after unfold);
controls overlap between shifted positions in the transposed op.
stride (s) and output padding (o)
• s is the key factor in how much Hout, Wout grow w.r.t. the input in many
designs.
• o is an extra 0-stride adjustment (separate from padding) to fix shape
mismatches when inverting a known conv/stride pattern (small integer,
often 0 or 1).

title: Numeric example: one spatial axis (H, dilation = 1)
text:
Numeric example: one spatial axis (H, dilation = 1)
Set-up
Hin = 7, k = 3, s = 2, p = 1, o = 1 (PyTorch: output padding on that
axis)
Formula
Hout = (Hin −1) · s −2p + (k −1) + o + 1 = (6) · 2 −2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 14 (per
axis).
Repetition
W uses the same k, s, p, o when it is a square, square-kernel, symmetric
padding (typical in segmentation blocks).

title: Literature: encoder–decoder (names only)
text:
Literature: encoder–decoder (names only)
Segmentation (semantic, instance variants)
• FCN (Long et al.): deconv (transposed) layers in the decoder to
upsample coarse score maps toward input resolution; skip-type fusion
appears in the hourglass family.
• U-Net (Ronneberger et al.): skip connections between encoder and
decoder; decoder often uses upconv / ConvTranspose2d-like blocks,
then concat with encoder, then 3 × 3 convs.
• DeepLab and others: sometimes combine transposed/stride approaches
with atrous context (different part of the course); still need high-res
logits for per-pixel class maps.
Practical
Same theme: get from low-res semantics to a mask aligned (or co-aligned)
with the input grid.

title: Keras / TensorFlow: Conv2DTranspose
text:
Keras / TensorFlow: Conv2DTranspose
Concept
• tf.keras.layers.Conv2DTranspose: similar role with arguments
filters, kernel size, strides, padding, output padding (naming
and defaults may differ slightly from PyTorch: always read the version
doc for exact shape rule).
• In segmentation heads, often stacked after encoder features.
Mental check
If Hout does not match the skip tensor you want to add/concat, adjust
padding, strides / output padding, or crop/pad the skip branch.

title: Bilinear (or nearest) + Conv2d vs ConvTranspose2d
text:
Bilinear (or nearest) + Conv2d vs ConvTranspose2d
Bilinear (fixed) + Conv2d
• Pros: no checkerboard from transposed striding; well-understood; strong
baselines in many decoders.
• Cons: upsample is not learned; capacity is in the follow-up Conv2d only.
Transposed conv (learned upsample)
• Pros: single op that jointly learns to expand and mix (flexible, widely
used in published nets).
• Cons: with poor init / stride choices, can contribute to checkerboard
patterns in the generated high-res field (Odena 2016); mitigations:
careful filter design, blend with bilinear, or post-smoothing.

• Cons: with poor init / stride choices, can contribute to checkerboard
patterns in the generated high-res field (Odena 2016); mitigations:
careful filter design, blend with bilinear, or post-smoothing.

title: Checkerboard (high level)
text:
Checkerboard (high level)
Where it comes from
If upsampling is implemented in a way that has uneven overlap between
shifted kernel placements, the effective “gain” of superposition can be
periodic, visible as a grid in feature maps (important in image generation as
well as some dense prediction curves).
In segmentation
Practical pipelines often: choose conservative stride/kernel/output padding,
use skip fusion, or add bilinear+conv blocks to reduce artifacts; treat this as
a known engineering concern, not a show-stopper.

title: Recap: where transposed conv fits
text:
Recap: where transposed conv fits
In the decoder
• Increases H and W (and transforms channels) in a learned way.
• Pairs with skip connections in many SOTA segmentation designs so that
localization (from encoder) and semantics (from the bottleneck)
combine.
To remember
• Not mathematical deconvolution (inverse filter).
• Do use the PyTorch/TF shape formulas to match your tensor layout
with encoder skips.

title: Summary
text:
Summary
Core ideas
• Segmentation = dense prediction: decoder must return to full (or target)
resolution.
• ConvTranspose2d = learnable upsampling (transposed of a strided
Conv2d in a precise sense).
• Key hyperparameters: k, s, p, output padding; verify Hout, Wout with
a tiny script.
• Alternatives: bilinear/nearest + Conv2d; often used to avoid
checkerboard issues.
• In U-Net–style models, shape-matching with skip connections is a main
engineering task.
